Game Story
⚑ Blotter Flag · Narrative Spine
The Blotter's Read called Shields to win rounds; she won the fight by TKO6 instead — the gap between the two is the story of how much faster she looked at 160 than her heavyweight tape suggested.
The Scouting Report Wrote the Ending
Claressa Shields, 31, stopped Kaye Scott, 42, in the sixth round to reclaim the WBC and WBA middleweight titles in front of a sold-out State Farm Arena — the first woman to headline the building.

Shields did what she came to do without needing a signature moment to explain it. Scott dropped her right hand in exchanges all night, and the left hook found that opening again and again — Shields sat down on her shots from the bell and opened a hematoma over Scott's eye in round one. The gap between them was always going to be fights, not years: Shields carries 95 documented bouts into this ring against Scott's 7, a difference no amount of amateur pedigree on Scott's side could close in one night. Scott showed a sturdy chin absorbing what she took, but she simply didn't have the tools for the job — a screwdriver and a hammer sent to dismantle a bridge.

The co-main carried a real grievance into the ring, not the usual weigh-in theater. Hicks won the 2020 Olympic Trials outright, but pandemic-scrambled qualification handed his seat to Isley anyway, based on 2019 rankings. Isley later beat that same opponent as a pro and turned it into fight-week trash talk aimed squarely at putting the Olympic story to rest. Hicks still maintains his only pro loss was a bad scorecard, not a real defeat — and at Friday's weigh-in the two had to be physically separated after jawing at each other on camera. It carried into the fight itself: referee Antonio Mohan stopped the action before round four just to lecture both corners, then docked Isley a point in round five for kidney punching. CompuBox tells its own version of the story — Isley and Hicks were separated by two or fewer landed punches in seven of the ten rounds, and Isley's biggest round of the fight, 17 of 54 landed, came immediately after the point deduction. He won it on volume in the end, throwing 132 more punches than the more accurate Hicks, taking all three cards clean (97-92, 96-93, 96-93) — but a fight built on that much real history never fully opened up the way it should have.

Round six, the same left hook that had been finding a home all night finally landed clean. Scott went down, beat the count, and kept fighting — until her corner had seen enough and put the towel in the air at 1:38. The night's most disputed result came later in the co-feature: Bernice Ferreira won the WBC and IBO super featherweight titles when Caroline Veyre was disqualified at 1:04 of round eight for excessive holding, her third infraction after point deductions in rounds four and seven. Referee Malik Waleed did too much here as well. Veyre's holding was real, and it was a repeat problem from her last title defense — Ferreira was clearly the faster fighter with better hands, pressing the action and boxing off the back foot early to set it up. But Veyre had no footwork to create space and no comfort fighting on the inside, and tying up was the only tool she had left. That's a fighter losing rounds on the cards, not one who needed to be thrown out of the ring — disqualifying a competitive title fight, with Veyre still live on the scorecards, was a heavier hammer than the offense called for.

Player Verdicts
Claressa ShieldsExceeded
Called to win rounds; won by sixth-round stoppage instead. Faster and more forceful at 160 than her heavyweight tape suggested.
Kaye ScottMissed
Never solved her tendency to drop the right hand in exchanges — Shields' left hook found that opening all night.
Troy IsleyDelivered
Won clean on all three cards as called, though a point deduction and a heavy-handed referee kept the fight from ever opening up.
Joseph HicksMissed
Hurt Isley early in round two but couldn't sustain it across ten rounds.
Ashleyann LozadaExceeded
No call was made pre-fight, but a five-fight professional dropping one round to a far more experienced opponent is a statement performance.
Atif OberltonDelivered
Called to stop Angulo; won a clean shutout decision instead — didn't get the finish, but answered the step-up test.
Bernice FerreiraDelivered
Faster hands, better skills, forced the fight throughout — won the titles regardless of how it technically ended.
Caroline VeyreMissed
Competitive on the cards, undone by a recurring, self-inflicted foul that cost her a second straight title fight.

Shields out-landed Scott 29 to 14 across the first two rounds, then Scott answered by trading in rounds three and four, landing 26 to Shields' 28. Shields pulled away in round five (22 landed to 15), dropped Scott in round six, and closed the fight on a barrage that drew the towel at 1:38. Scott finished with the higher connect percentage on lower volume — consistent with a fighter who had to take chances rather than control range.
Card-Wide Results · Blotter Call vs. Result
Isley (dark blue) vs. Hicks · State Farm Arena, Atlanta · Photo credit Kwesi Kotoko
Troy Isley (17-0) vs. Joseph Hicks (12-2)
Isley UD10
Called: Isley by decision. HIT — winner and method. This carried a real grievance, not manufactured beef: Hicks won the 2020 Trials outright but lost his Olympic seat to Isley on a pandemic-scrambled qualification call, and the two had to be separated at Friday's weigh-in. CompuBox had it far tighter than the judges did — Isley 103/382 (27%), Hicks 99/250 (39.6%), separated by two or fewer landed punches in seven of ten rounds — and Isley's biggest round came right after his point deduction for kidney punching in round five.
Bernice Ferreira (11-0) vs. Caroline Veyre (11-2)
Ferreira DQ8
Called: Veyre by decision. MISS — wrong winner. Ferreira's speed and pressure were undersold pre-fight; Veyre's holding problem, flagged from her last title defense, finally cost her the belt outright.
Atif Oberlton (17-0) vs. Roamer Alexis Angulo (29-5)
Oberlton UD10
Called: Oberlton by stoppage. Winner HIT, method MISS — a clean shutout decision (100-90 across the board) over a two-time world title challenger, but no finish.
Ashleyann Lozada (5-0) vs. Paulette Valenzuela Cuesta (19-6-1)
Lozada UD10
No lean was called pre-fight. Lozada dropped a single round across three scorecards, landing 130 of 220 punches to Cuesta's 55 of 130 — a five-fight professional already fighting like she belongs several levels up.
Da'Velle Smith (15-0) vs. Hakim Lopez (16-2)
Smith TKO6
Called: Lopez by decision. MISS — wrong winner. Smith stopped Lopez on cuts and volume rather than the competitive decision the pre-fight lean expected.
Shannel Butler (9-0) vs. Marianela Soledad Ramirez (14-12-2)
Butler UD8
Called: Butler by decision or late stoppage. HIT — winner and method, straightforward as projected (78-74, 78-74, 79-72).
Jaquan McElroy (8-0) vs. Alexander Thiel (5-1)
McElroy UD6
No lean was called pre-fight. McElroy swept all three cards 58-56.
Daniel Mercado (2-0) vs. Rahmel McKinley (1-5)
Mercado KO1
Called: Mercado, heavy favorite. HIT on the winner — first-round knockout, 1:48.
Casey Dixon (7-0) vs. Michael Nelson (4-3-1)
Unconfirmed
Called: Dixon by decision. Result unreported as of print — no source, including BoxRec's own event listing, has published an outcome. Not graded; dash stands until a result surfaces.
Danielle Perkins (6-1) vs. Olivia Curry (7-3-2)
Scrapped
Perkins missed weight by four pounds for her WBA light heavyweight title defense; the bout was pulled from the card, as flagged in the pre-fight program.

Honest miss acknowledgment: the co-main pick undersold Ferreira's hand speed and pressure and missed a repeat foul pattern from Veyre's own prior title defense. The main-event and Oberlton-Angulo method misses both trace to the same root cause — not weighting how much faster both fighters looked in-ring than their tape projected. Logged to the permanent lesson file.
Claressa Shields
A Sixth Reign, a Fifth Weight Class, and a Building Now Hers

Shields becomes the first woman to headline State Farm Arena, turning a road environment into a hometown-feeling night through her "In Her Corner" community work, and adds a sixth title reign at a fifth weight class. The GWOAT claim gets harder to argue with every outing.

Troy Isley & Joseph Hicks
The Grievance Is Settled — The Title Shot Is Next

Isley stays unbeaten at 17-0 and closes the loop on the Olympic story that's followed him since 2020 — a clean win over the man who felt wronged by it. He's now firmly in position for a world title opportunity; the punch stats ran tighter than the scorecards suggested, but the record and résumé both point the same direction. Hicks, still 12-2, has to find another way to make his case.

Ashleyann Lozada
Five Fights In, Ready for the Level That Usually Takes a Decade

An Olympic pedigree showing up in the pro ranks immediately. Five fights in, she's already fighting like she belongs several levels up the ladder.

Bernice Ferreira & Caroline Veyre
A Title Win With an Asterisk, a Second Straight Foul-Marred Loss

Ferreira's title win will always carry a footnote for how it ended, deserved belt or not. Veyre now has back-to-back title fights compromised by the same foul — a pattern, not a one-off, and one she'll need to fix before her next shot.
